title: Codes on Stones and in Books
bigQuestion: How can a message be hidden in plain sight, and how do people figure out what it says?

story.title: Shapes on an Old Stone
story.kicker: A visitor in a busy New York churchyard spots a row of strange shapes carved on a gravestone.
paragraphs: It is a bright fall day in New York City. Tall office towers rise on every side. Cars and buses rush along Broadway. A girl we will call Rosa walks through a gate with her aunt. Suddenly the street noise feels far away. They are in Trinity Churchyard, one of the oldest burial grounds in the city.

Old gray gravestones lean in the grass. Most of them show names and dates. Rosa stops at one small stone. It belongs to a man named James Leeson. He died in 1794. Near the top is a carving of a square and a compass. Rosa's aunt says that is a sign of the Freemasons, a very old club of friends.

Then Rosa sees something odd. Along one edge is a row of little shapes. Some look like boxes with open sides. Some look like the letter V turned in different ways. A few have tiny dots inside. "Is that a secret language?" Rosa asks. Her aunt smiles. "It is a code. And we can learn to read it."

Rosa's aunt draws two tic-tac-toe grids and two big X shapes in a notebook. She writes letters of the alphabet inside the spaces. Rosa matches the first shape on the stone to a space in the grid. It is the letter R. Then E. Then M. Letter by letter, a message appears.

Rosa is a made-up visitor. But the stone is real. You can still see it in the churchyard today. In this chapter, you will learn the code that is carved on it. You will also learn how people break codes they have never seen before.
story.think: Why do you think someone would carve a message in code on a gravestone, where anyone can see it?

lessons.title: Letters in Little Pens
lessons.mainIdea: The pigpen cipher swaps each letter for the shape of the space it sits in on a grid or an X.
reading: Picture a farm. Pigs live in small fenced areas called pens. The *pigpen cipher* gets its name from that idea. Each letter of the alphabet lives in its own little pen. To write a letter in code, you draw the shape of its pen instead of the letter.

Here is one common way to set it up. Draw a tic-tac-toe grid and put A through I in its nine spaces. Draw a second grid with a dot in each space for J through R. Then draw a big X for S, T, U and V. A second X with dots holds W, X, Y and Z.

Now look at the letter A. It sits in the top left corner of the first grid. Its pen has a line on the right and a line on the bottom. So A is written as a shape like a backward L. Every letter gets a shape this way. There are other versions of the key, so the letters may sit in a different order.

words.d: a secret alphabet where each letter is written as the shape of its space on a grid or an X
a way of hiding a message by changing each letter into another letter or symbol

look.title: Draw the Key
look.text: Draw a tic-tac-toe grid. Write A, B, C in the top row, D, E, F in the middle row and G, H, I in the bottom row. Look at the middle space, where E lives. It has lines on all four sides. So in pigpen, E is written as a small closed box.
look.prompt: Using the same grid, what shape would you draw for the letter C? Describe which sides have lines.

check.q: Where does the pigpen cipher get its name?
choices: From a famous code maker named Pig
From pens on a farm, because each letter sits in its own little pen
From the pens people use for writing
check.why: The reading says the name comes from farm pens. Each letter lives in its own pen, or space.

check.q: In pigpen, what do you draw instead of a letter?
choices: The shape of the letter's space on the grid or X
check.why: In the pigpen cipher, each letter is written as the shape of the space it sits in.

check.q: In the common key, how is the second grid different from the first grid?
choices: It has a dot in each space
It has no lines at all
It is shaped like a star
check.why: The reading says the second grid has a dot in each space. The dots show that the letter comes from J through R.

lessons.title: An Old Idea, a Masonic Name
lessons.mainIdea: Pigpen is older than the Freemasons, but Freemasons used it so much that it is often called the Masonic cipher.
reading: Many people say the Freemasons invented pigpen. The *Freemasons* are a brotherhood that began with stonemasons, the workers who built with stone. Their lodges, or clubs, grew in Britain in the 1600s and 1700s. But the idea of hiding letters in a grid is older than their lodges.

In the 1530s, a German writer named Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa published a big book about hidden knowledge. Scholars agree it shows letters placed in a grid of boxes. Historians see this grid as an early ancestor of pigpen. That book came out long before the first grand lodge of Freemasons.

So the Freemasons did not invent the grid. They took it up and spread it. Masons used it widely from the 1700s. That is why pigpen is also called the Masonic cipher or the Freemasons' cipher. A name can tell you who used a thing most, not who made it first.

words.d: a brotherhood that grew out of groups of stonemasons; its members meet in lodges
an older thing or person that a newer one comes from

look.title: Two Claims Side by Side
look.text: Claim 1: "The Freemasons invented the pigpen cipher." Claim 2: "A grid for hiding letters appears in Agrippa's book from the 1530s. Freemasons used a version of it widely from the 1700s."
look.prompt: Which claim fits the evidence of dates better? Explain how the dates help you decide.

check.q: Why is pigpen sometimes called the Masonic cipher?
choices: Because a Mason carved the first one in 1530
Because it is only allowed inside lodges
Because Freemasons used it widely from the 1700s
Because it uses the square and compass
check.why: The reading says Masons took up the cipher and used it widely, so it got their name.

check.q: What does Agrippa's book from the 1530s show?
choices: Letters placed in a grid of boxes
check.why: Scholars agree Agrippa's book shows letters in a grid, an early ancestor of pigpen.

check.q: What lesson about names does this story teach?
choices: A name always tells who made a thing
Names of codes are always secret
A name can tell who used a thing most, not who made it first
check.why: The Masonic cipher is named for the Masons who used it, even though the grid idea is older.

lessons.title: Codes and Ciphers
lessons.mainIdea: A code swaps whole words, a cipher swaps letters, and both turn plain words into hidden ones.
reading: People often say "code" for any secret message. Codebreakers use two words. A *code* swaps a whole word or idea for something else. For example, a team might agree that "pizza" means "meet at the gym." You need the list of meanings to understand it.

A cipher works on single letters. Each letter is changed into another letter or a symbol. Pigpen is a cipher, because every letter gets its own shape. You can hide any word with a cipher, even a word nobody planned for.

The message you start with is called *plaintext*. It is the plain words anyone can read. After you hide it, it is called ciphertext. Changing plaintext into ciphertext is called enciphering. Changing it back is called deciphering. Many people also say encode and decode.

words.d: a system that swaps whole words or ideas for other words or signs
the message in plain words before it is hidden
the message after it has been hidden with a cipher

look.title: Code or Cipher?
look.text: Message A: A coach tells the team that "blue" means "run to the left." Message B: A student writes her name with every letter turned into a pigpen shape.
look.prompt: Which message uses a code, and which uses a cipher? What clue helped you tell them apart?

check.q: What is the difference between a code and a cipher?
choices: A code uses numbers and a cipher uses colors
A code swaps whole words, and a cipher swaps single letters
A code is new and a cipher is very old
There is no difference at all
check.why: The reading says a code swaps whole words or ideas, and a cipher changes each letter.

check.q: What is plaintext?
choices: A message written on plain paper
A message that has been hidden
The message in plain words before it is hidden
check.why: Plaintext is the plain message anyone can read, before it is hidden.

check.q: Why is pigpen called a cipher and not a code?
choices: Because every single letter gets its own shape
Because it only works for one word
Because it was made by a coach
Because it uses a list of meanings
check.why: Pigpen changes each letter into a shape, which is what a cipher does.

lessons.title: A Stone in Trinity Churchyard
lessons.mainIdea: James Leeson, who died in 1794, has a gravestone in New York with a line carved in the pigpen cipher.
reading: Trinity Church stands on Broadway at Wall Street in Lower Manhattan. Around it is an old churchyard, a burial ground next to a church. People have been buried there since the 1600s. Today it sits among tall office buildings.

One stone belongs to James Leeson, who died in 1794. The stone shows a square and a compass. That is a well-known *symbol* of the Freemasons. It tells us Leeson was likely a Mason, or his friends wanted to honor the Masons. The stone also has other carvings often seen on old graves.

Across the stone runs a line of small shapes. They are letters in the pigpen cipher. Anyone who knows the key can read them. Many visitors walk right past without noticing. That is part of what makes it a good *mystery* for a codebreaker.

words.d: a picture or shape that stands for an idea or a group
something that is hard to understand or not yet explained

look.title: The Leeson Gravestone
look.text: A small upright gravestone for James Leeson, who died in 1794. It is carved with the Masonic square and compass and other grave carvings. A line of pigpen shapes runs across it. When decoded, the shapes read REMEMBER DEATH.
look.cite: James Leeson gravestone, Trinity Churchyard, New York, 1794 (described from photographs; see Atlas Obscura, "Trinity Churchyard")
look.prompt: Which parts of this stone could anyone understand, and which part needs a key? Explain.

check.q: Where is James Leeson's gravestone?
choices: In Trinity Churchyard in New York City
check.why: The reading says the stone is in the churchyard of Trinity Church, on Broadway at Wall Street.

check.q: What does the square and compass on the stone stand for?
check.why: The reading says the square and compass is a well-known symbol of the Freemasons.

check.q: Who can read the line of shapes on the stone?
choices: Anyone who knows the pigpen key
No one, because it has never been solved
check.why: The shapes are pigpen letters, so anyone who knows the key can read them.

lessons.title: Remember Death
lessons.mainIdea: The pigpen line on the Leeson stone reads REMEMBER DEATH, an old reminder that life is short and precious.
reading: When you decode the shapes on the Leeson stone, they spell REMEMBER DEATH. You can check this yourself. Match each shape to its pen in the key. The letters line up one by one. Many writers and codebreakers have checked it the same way.

The words may sound gloomy at first. But they were a very common message in those days. People called this kind of reminder by a Latin name, *memento mori*. It means "remember that you will die." The idea was to live well, be kind and use your time wisely.

Old gravestones in Europe and America often carried this message. Some showed an hourglass, with sand running out. Leeson's stone says the same thing in a quieter way. Only people who knew the cipher could read it at a glance.

words.d: Latin words meaning "remember that you will die"; a reminder to live well
to turn a hidden message back into plain words

look.title: Letters in the Stone's Message
look.cite: Letter count of the decoded line REMEMBER DEATH, James Leeson gravestone, Trinity Churchyard, New York (1794)
look.prompt: Which letter shows up most in this short message? Why might that help a codebreaker who did not have the key?

check.q: What does the pigpen line on the Leeson stone say?
check.why: When the shapes are decoded with the key, they spell REMEMBER DEATH.

check.q: What does memento mori mean?
check.why: The reading says memento mori is Latin for remember that you will die.

check.q: What was the goal of a memento mori message?
choices: To scare children away from graves
To remind people to live well and use their time wisely
To hide the location of treasure
To give directions to the church
check.why: The reading says the idea was to live well, be kind and use time wisely.

lessons.title: Why Put Code on a Grave?
lessons.mainIdea: A cipher on a gravestone can be a message for friends who share a secret, not a treasure clue.
reading: A gravestone is public. Anyone can walk by and look. So why carve words that most people cannot read? We do not have a letter from Leeson or his friends that explains it. Historians can only look at the clues.

One clue is the square and compass. Masons in the 1700s knew the pigpen cipher well. A line in pigpen could be a quiet message to fellow Masons. It said, in effect, "This man was one of us." It was a way of belonging, like a team handshake.

Some people online claim the stone hides a treasure map. There is no evidence for that. The decoded words are a common saying about life and death. When a message is solved, it is wise to trust what the letters say. A good *historian* asks for evidence before believing an exciting story.

words.d: a person who studies the past using evidence
facts or objects that help show whether something is true

look.title: Two Visitors Talk
look.text: Visitor 1: "This code must hide the way to buried gold!" Visitor 2: "The code says REMEMBER DEATH. That was a common grave saying. The Masonic symbol suggests it was a message for other Masons."
look.prompt: Which visitor uses evidence? Point to one fact each visitor gives or leaves out.

check.q: Why might Masons have used pigpen on Leeson's stone?
choices: To hide the way to gold
To keep the church from reading it
As a quiet message to fellow Masons who knew the cipher
Because they could not spell in English
check.why: The reading says a pigpen line could be a quiet message to other Masons, a way of belonging.

check.q: Is there evidence that the Leeson stone hides a treasure map?
choices: No, the decoded words are a common saying
Yes, the church found the gold
Yes, Leeson wrote a letter about it
No, because the stone has no carvings
check.why: The reading says there is no evidence for a treasure map. The words are a common saying about life and death.

check.q: What does a good historian do before believing an exciting story?
choices: Tells it to as many people as possible
Waits for someone famous to agree
check.why: The reading says a good historian asks for evidence first.

lessons.title: Substitution Ciphers
lessons.mainIdea: In a substitution cipher, every letter is swapped for another letter or symbol by the same rule.
reading: To substitute means to put one thing in place of another. A *substitution cipher* puts a new letter or symbol in place of each letter. Pigpen is a substitution cipher. Each letter is always swapped for the same shape.

A very old example comes from ancient Rome. The Roman writer Suetonius wrote about the life of Julius Caesar. He said Caesar sent private letters in a cipher. Each letter was moved a few places down the alphabet. Today this is called a *shift cipher*, or the Caesar cipher.

Here is how a shift of three works. A becomes D. B becomes E. C becomes F. So the word CAT becomes FDW. To read it, you shift each letter back three places. The rule is simple, and it stays the same for the whole message.

words.d: a cipher that swaps each letter for another letter or symbol, always by the same rule
a cipher that moves each letter the same number of places along the alphabet

look.title: A Roman Writer on Caesar's Letters
look.text: When Caesar had something private to say, he wrote it in cipher. He changed the order of the letters so no word could be made out. To read it, you put D in place of A, and do the same with the other letters.
look.cite: Suetonius, The Life of Julius Caesar (in The Lives of the Caesars), c. 121 CE
look.prompt: How many places did Caesar shift each letter? Use the clue about A and D to explain.

check.q: In a shift cipher with a shift of three, what does A become?
check.why: With a shift of three, A moves three places to D.

check.q: Who wrote about Caesar using a cipher?
check.why: The reading says the Roman writer Suetonius described Caesar's letters in cipher.

check.q: Why is pigpen a substitution cipher?
choices: Because each letter is always swapped for the same shape
Because it shifts letters by three
Because it was used in Rome
check.why: A substitution cipher swaps each letter by the same rule, and pigpen gives each letter the same shape every time.

lessons.title: The Key Opens the Lock
lessons.mainIdea: A key is the rule or chart that locks a message and unlocks it again, so it must be kept safe.
reading: Think of a locked diary. The lock keeps the pages private. The key opens it. A cipher works the same way. The *key* is the rule or chart that hides the message and brings it back.

For a shift cipher, the key is a number, like three. For pigpen, the key is the drawing of the grids and X shapes. The person sending the message and the person getting it both need the same key. Anyone else should not have it.

Here is a problem. The pigpen key has been printed in many books. Today almost anyone can find it. So pigpen hides a message only from people who have not learned it. A cipher is only as strong as the secret of its key.

words.d: the rule, number or chart used to hide a message and to read it again
to hide a message by turning its letters into cipher letters or symbols

look.title: Two Friends and a Key
look.text: Jada and Luis make a secret shift cipher. They agree on the key "five" at recess. Later, Jada writes a note using a shift of five. A classmate finds the note. He does not know the key, so he tries a shift of one, then two, then three.
look.prompt: How many tries might the classmate need to find the key? What could Jada and Luis do to make their cipher harder to break?

check.q: What is the key in a cipher?
choices: The first word of the message
The paper the message is written on
The person who breaks the code
The rule or chart used to hide and read the message
check.why: The reading says the key is the rule or chart that hides the message and brings it back.

check.q: Why is pigpen not very safe today?
choices: Its key has been printed in many books
It only works in New York
It can only be carved in stone
check.why: The reading says the pigpen key is printed in many books, so almost anyone can find it.

check.q: What is the key for a shift cipher?
check.why: The reading says the key for a shift cipher is a number that tells how far to move each letter.

lessons.title: Counting Letters
lessons.mainIdea: Some letters appear much more often than others, and counting them helps codebreakers crack a cipher.
reading: About 1,100 years ago, a scholar named al-Kindi lived in Baghdad. He wrote the oldest known guide to breaking ciphers. His big idea was to count. In any long piece of writing, some letters show up much more than others.

In English, the most common letter is E. Codebreakers measure it at about 12.7 out of every 100 letters. Next come T, A and O. Letters like Q and Z are rare. Counting how often each letter appears is called *frequency analysis*. Frequency means how often something happens.

Here is how it helps. Say a secret message uses the shape of a triangle more than any other symbol. That triangle probably stands for E. The codebreaker writes E above each triangle. One guess at a time, the message starts to open.

words.d: breaking a cipher by counting how often each letter or symbol appears
how often something happens

look.title: The Most Common Letters in English
look.cite: Robert Lewand, Cryptological Mathematics (Mathematical Association of America, 2000), English letter frequency table
look.prompt: About how many times more common is E than Z? What would you guess first if a symbol appeared a lot in a secret message?

check.q: Which letter is the most common in English?
check.why: The reading says E is the most common letter in English, about 12.7 out of every 100 letters.

check.q: Who wrote the oldest known guide to breaking ciphers?
check.why: The reading says al-Kindi of Baghdad wrote the oldest known guide to breaking ciphers.

check.q: If one symbol appears most often in a long English message, what letter does it probably stand for?
check.why: Frequency analysis says the most common symbol probably stands for E, the most common English letter.

lessons.title: Clues From Short Words
lessons.mainIdea: Codebreakers mix letter counts with clues from short words and patterns to test their guesses.
reading: Counting letters is a great start, but it is not the whole job. Short messages can trick you. In REMEMBER DEATH, E is most common, which fits. But a short note about a zoo might have lots of Z and O. So codebreakers look for more clues.

Short words are strong clues. In English, a one-letter word is almost always A or I. A common three-letter word is THE. If a message has the same three symbols again and again, they may spell THE. Then you know T, H and E all at once.

Codebreakers also look for *patterns*. A double symbol, like in the middle of LOOK or BALL, is often O, E, L, S or T. Each guess is tested against the whole message. If a guess makes real words, keep it. If not, try again. Mistakes are part of the work.

words.d: something that repeats in a way you can notice and use
trying an answer, testing it, and changing it if it does not work

look.title: A Three-Symbol Clue
look.text: A secret message has the symbol group star, moon, box five times. Each time it stands alone as a three-letter word. The box is also the most common symbol in the whole message.
look.prompt: What word might star, moon, box spell? Which three letters would you now know? Explain your thinking.

check.q: In English, a one-letter word is almost always which letter?
check.why: The reading says a one-letter word in English is almost always A or I.

check.q: Why can counting letters trick you in a short message?
choices: Short messages may not follow the usual pattern
Short messages cannot be written in pigpen
Short messages always use a key
check.why: The reading gives the example of a short note about a zoo, which might have lots of Z and O.

check.q: What should a codebreaker do if a guess does not make real words?
check.why: The reading says to test each guess. If it does not make real words, try again.

lessons.title: Make and Break a Code Together
lessons.mainIdea: Codebreaking works best as teamwork, where each person spots different clues and checks the others' guesses.
reading: Now it is your turn. Your class can split into two teams. Team One makes a message. They choose a short sentence, maybe ten to fifteen words. They pick a cipher, such as a shift cipher or their own symbol alphabet. They keep the key hidden.

Team Two gets only the ciphertext. First, they count each symbol and make a tally chart. Next, they look for one-letter words and repeating groups. One person can track guesses on the board. Another can read the message aloud as it changes.

Real codebreakers work in teams too. One person may be good at counting. Another may notice patterns or know many words. When the message is solved, both teams can talk. What made it hard? What gave it away? *Teamwork* makes both sides stronger.

words.d: a chart that uses marks to count how many times something appears
people working together, each adding their own strengths

look.title: Plan Your Code Challenge
look.text: Team One writes the plaintext: I LIKE TO READ BOOKS AT THE LIBRARY. They choose a shift of four. Team Two will get only the ciphertext. They will have a tally chart, the board and a timer that is turned off, so no one feels rushed.
look.prompt: What clue do you think Team Two will spot first? Name one short word or pattern that could give the message away.

check.q: What does Team Two get at the start of the challenge?
check.why: The reading says Team Two gets only the ciphertext and must break it.

check.q: What is a tally chart used for in codebreaking?
choices: Counting how many times each symbol appears
check.why: A tally chart counts how often each symbol appears, which is the first step of frequency analysis.

check.q: Why do codebreakers often work in teams?
choices: Each person can spot different clues
One person is never allowed to read a cipher
Teams do not need to check guesses
check.why: The reading says one person may be good at counting and another at noticing patterns, so teamwork helps.

review.q: How do you write a letter in the pigpen cipher?
choices: Draw the shape of the letter's space on the grid or X
Write the next letter in the alphabet
Write a number for the letter
review.why: In pigpen, each letter is written as the shape of its pen, or space, on the key.

review.q: Which statement about the history of pigpen fits the evidence?
choices: Julius Caesar invented it in Rome
It was first carved on the Leeson stone
A grid for letters appears in the 1530s, and Masons later used it widely
review.why: Agrippa's book from the 1530s shows a letter grid. Masons took it up and spread it from the 1700s.

review.q: What does the pigpen line on James Leeson's stone say?
review.why: Decoded with the key, the line reads REMEMBER DEATH, a memento mori message.

review.q: What is the difference between plaintext and ciphertext?
choices: Plaintext is in pigpen and ciphertext is in English
Plaintext is the plain message and ciphertext is the hidden one
Plaintext is typed and ciphertext is handwritten
review.why: Plaintext is the message before it is hidden. Ciphertext is the message after it is hidden.

review.q: In a shift cipher with a shift of three, what does the word CAT become?
review.why: Each letter moves three places: C to F, A to D, T to W. So CAT becomes FDW.

review.q: What did al-Kindi teach codebreakers to do?
review.why: al-Kindi of Baghdad wrote about counting letters, which we now call frequency analysis.

review.q: A long English message in cipher uses one symbol far more than any other. What is the best first guess?
choices: It is a space and means nothing
review.why: E is the most common letter in English, so the most common symbol probably stands for E.

review.q: Why is it wise to ask for evidence before believing that a code hides treasure?
choices: Because exciting stories are not always true, and evidence shows what is
Because historians do not like stories
review.why: The Leeson stone lesson shows that the decoded words, not the exciting story, are the evidence.
